turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is really interesting because again, I think Atlassian is one of the very few companies that has done this so well. And I don't know, this number is absurd. I've never heard of another company that's 15 successful products. I don't know how successful they're, but they're out there and people seem to be... They're being promoted. I guess is there any other advice to share along the lines of if someone is thinking about launching a second product, anything you would suggest they do or think about they may not be thinking about?
turns.zh: 这真的很有趣，因为我认为Atlassian是少数做得非常好的公司之一。我不知道，这个数字太惊人了。我从未听说过有其他公司推出了15款成功的产品。我不知道它们有多成功，但它们确实存在，人们似乎……它们正在被推广。我猜有没有其他建议可以分享给那些考虑推出第二款产品的人，比如你会建议他们做什么或者考虑什么他们可能没有考虑过的事情？

turns.speaker: Megan Cook
turns.en: I think my advice is skied towards the Atlassian case, which is where you're in a 12,000 strong employee company and how do you seed something that you want to run as more with more of a startup kind of mindset. So when you get to this size, you've got quarterly planning and business reviews and all of these different process and you don't necessarily want to put your seed startup through that. It's not quite ready for that kind of thing. So I think the key things here that make it really successful is starting really small with the idea and the solution to be proved and don't add too many people, don't feel pressured to add too many people. I think it's easy to get really excited about the potential and just want to throw four or five teams at it, but that can... We were talking about this stat. That can make things run slower and so you want to protect them. (00:56:39): And the second thing is just give them freedom to move really fast and solve those problems in a different way. So there are different expectations. They don't necessarily need to be a part of that process that I was talking about before. This team should just be running hard to prove whether or not the idea's going to work and whether there's product market fit. (00:56:59): And for different approaches. If I want to add something to Jira software, but we're talking millions and millions of users there, that thing has to be resilient. It's got to scale. There are all these things that users inherently expect from something like that. But for something small like this, we are proving product market fit. You don't need to think about that initially. So you've got to hold this to a different standard, otherwise you're just going to slow them down way too much. (00:57:25): And actually we found that by letting them tackle problems a little differently, we found innovative way of looking at things that we can pull back into our other products. So for example, if you look at Jira Product Discovery, and just the way that it gives more of a spreadsheet kind of view of a list of ideas and things like that, some of the experience there is definitely something that we'll be pulling into Jira software.
turns.zh:
我认为我的建议主要针对Atlassian的案例——在一家拥有1.2万名员工的公司中，如何以更具创业精神的思维方式推动新项目的落地。当公司规模达到一定规模后，季度规划、业务评估等流程会变得复杂，而新项目可能尚未准备好应对这些繁琐的程序。因此，关键在于以极小规模验证创意和解决方案，避免过早扩充团队。人们很容易被项目潜力冲昏头脑，一股脑地投入四五个团队，但这样做往往会拖慢进度。（00:56:39）  
第二点是给予团队快速行动的自由，允许他们以不同方式解决问题。团队无需遵循之前提到的那些流程，只需全力验证创意是否可行、是否符合产品市场匹配度。（00:56:59）  
对于不同项目而言，若想在Jira软件中添加新功能，但面对数百万用户，这项创新必须具备高可靠性和扩展性。这些用户对此类产品的期望本就很高。而对于小型项目，我们只需验证产品市场匹配度即可，无需过早考虑这些复杂问题。（00:57:25）  
实际上，我们发现通过让团队以不同方式解决问题，可以挖掘出创新的思路，这些思路还能反哺到其他产品中。例如，Jira产品探索功能以电子表格形式呈现创意列表，其中的某些体验元素将被引入Jira软件。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned that over the years, Jira has weathered many storms. From my perspective, it feels like it continues to weather many storms incredibly well. One, because there's just endless startups always coming at Jira trying to become the new project management tool that everyone uses. And two, it just feels like people are always dissing on Jira like, "Jira sucks, I want to use something else." On the other hand, it continues to dominate. Many people love it. I'm curious what you believe Atlassian generally has done and your team has done to keep Jira ahead of everyone. And I know you're probably going to say, "We listen to customers better than anyone." So if that's a big part of the answer, definitely share that. But I'm curious, is there anything else people may not be recognizing of just why Jira has been so successful for so long?
turns.zh: 你提到多年来Jira经受了诸多挑战。在我看来，它似乎始终能出色地应对风雨。一方面，源源不断的初创公司试图取代Jira成为新的项目管理工具；另一方面，用户总在吐槽“Jira太烂了，我想换别的用”。但Jira始终占据主导地位，深受用户喜爱。我很好奇Atlassian整体上以及你的团队为保持Jira领先地位做了哪些努力。我猜你可能会说：“我们比任何人都更倾听客户需求。” 如果这确实是关键因素，欢迎分享。但我更想了解，是否还有其他不为人知的成功秘诀？

turns.speaker: Megan Cook
turns.en: Yeah. I think the number of startups that enter this space, just so it shows how important the problem is that we solve and that problem of teamwork and collaboration. We've got more than 125,000 customers around the world who start their day in Jira, millions of users and the kinds of companies that use it. I just love hearing about what they do with it. They really blow me away. Like NASA landing the Mars rover or Canva building this design platform for 40 million people, it's just massive.
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得进入这个领域的初创公司数量，恰恰说明了我们所解决的问题有多重要，还有团队协作和合作的问题。我们在全球拥有超过12.5万名客户，他们每天都从Jira开始工作，有数百万用户，还有许多大公司在使用它。我特别喜欢听他们讲述如何利用Jira创造价值。他们的成果总是让我惊叹不已。比如NASA成功着陆火星探测器，或者Canva为4000万用户打造设计平台，这些成就都堪称非凡。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't think you can beat that Mars rover story array. That's a good one. I think when you follow it up with the Canvas story, that one's less interesting now, but it's also amazing. Okay. Sorry. Keep going.
turns.zh: 我觉得没人能比得上火星探测器的故事。这真是个绝佳的案例。接着再讲Canva的故事，虽然现在听起来没那么吸引人了，但依然令人惊叹。好的，抱歉，请继续分享。

turns.speaker: Megan Cook
turns.en: So like you said, they are integral to our success. We do obsess over them. We think if we do right by them, then we're going to be going in the right direction. I don't think we've ever had this sense of arrogance of just... No matter how big we are, we've always got this healthy dose of paranoia that we need to keep working on improving things and being better. So to your point about customer feedback, that is a big part of it. We bake in these rituals just to make it super easy for everyone to do that. So the whole company gets an email every week and it's just got a random selection of feedback from our customers. It's got how they rate us and just a quote as well. And so everyone's sort of getting this dose of feedback all the time. (01:00:24): We have regular share outs of all of the research that everyone gets. We get in-product feedback. We make it super easy to talk to our customers through social media or LinkedIn or X now. And then we also have a whole community space where customers can have longer conversations with us about different ideas that we're coming up with or feedback that they have for us. So I think that is all massively important for keeping Jira ahead of the pack. (01:00:58): I think how we stay ahead in other areas is just that the culture is super, super open to innovation, kind of invites innovation. So we have these hackathons, we call them shepherd. The whole company stops and everyone can play with new ideas or technologies. It's a competition. So the best ideas get visibility. It can get people working with other people that they wouldn't normally. And also the visibility of the ideas helps generate more ideas all over the place. (01:01:31): Like I said before, innovation can come from anywhere. So anyone can pitch new ideas or products. And when we see new technologies emerging that we think are going to be really foundational and interesting, we'll carve off a team to go and look at that. So I think we've had an AI team central to Atlassian for a long time, but with the advent of ChatGPT, there's sort of this huge move forward. There's this leak that's happening. And so in my team, I just carved off a small team to go and explore that and see what interesting things that we could do there. (01:02:09): I think we don't shy away from tackling subsets of the market that we're seeing that need a bit more love, like the Jira Product Discovery story that we were just talking about a second ago. And we also use our products a lot and that helps us find all of those little problems and makes it really real. We get really excited about the different things that the whole team is working on. We send lots of feedback to each other. I think that's also a really important part of it. (01:02:42): Another area is when we look at how we're investing, there's always this pressure to invest in the core business, of course, but we also make sure that we invest in seeding future businesses. And like we're talking about, they might not always work out. So we had then the Compass and the Atlas example of ones that have worked out, but we also see things through Atlassian inventions. So if there are interesting ideas or technologies, these might support the products later on, that's something that we'll go and seed out there in the market. And that's led to a few acquisitions there as well, which has been really useful. (01:03:21): And the last thing is I think I am just really impressed at the way that we stay agile to move towards these different shifts that come up. It always surprises me just how agile we can be. For example, in 2020 we decided to double down on our mission to deliver a world-class cloud experience. And it was like hundreds of people just moved around in Atlassian to make that happen, which was in a very short period of time, which was impressive. And we're not shy about killing things off with their [inaudible 01:03:55]. So I'll give you another example of one of those products that was going through that we ended up killing off. So we had a whiteboard product that we thought would be its own product, sort of like a Jira Product Discovery. And when we came to one of those gates with the team, we realized actually this is more a really useful document type. And so now you'll see that it's a feature in Confluence. It was very quick to make that decision.
turns.zh:
正如你所说，他们对我们的成功至关重要。我们确实对他们十分上心。我们认为，只要我们能做好，就能朝着正确的方向前进。我认为我们从未有过那种自大的感觉——无论我们规模多大，始终保持着健康的警惕感，持续努力改进和提升。说到客户反馈，这确实是关键一环。我们设计了诸多反馈机制，让每个人都能轻松参与其中。比如每周全公司都会收到邮件，里面随机抽取了客户的反馈内容，包括他们的评分和引用语句。这样每个人都能时刻接收到反馈信息。（01:00:24）我们会定期分享所有研究成果，收集产品内反馈，并通过社交媒体、领英等平台与客户保持沟通。此外，我们还专门搭建了社区平台，让客户能与我们深入探讨新想法或提供反馈。我认为这些举措对Jira保持领先地位至关重要。  （01:00:58）在其他创新领域，我们的文化极其开放，鼓励创新。例如，我们举办名为"Shepherd"的黑客马拉松活动，整个公司暂停工作，员工可以自由探索新技术或新创意。这是一场竞赛，优秀的创意会获得曝光机会，推动跨部门合作，同时反馈信息能激发更多创新火花。  （01:01:31）正如我之前所说，创新可能来自任何地方。任何人都能提出新想法或新产品。当我们发现新兴技术可能成为基础性突破时，就会组建团队进行探索。比如人工智能团队在Atlassian内部就存在已久，但ChatGPT的出现带来了巨大变革。我们的团队迅速组建小团队进行探索，寻找可应用的场景。  （01:02:09）我们从不回避那些需要特别关注的细分市场，比如我们刚刚讨论的Jira产品发现案例。我们还深度使用自家产品，及时发现问题并激发团队热情。我们会互相分享反馈，这也是关键所在。  （01:02:42）在投资策略上，我们始终坚持核心业务优先，同时布局未来业务。以Compass和Atlas的成功案例为例，我们也通过Atlassian内部创新来孕育新项目。只要有有趣的技术或想法，都有可能为现有产品赋能，这正是我们在市场上布局种子项目的逻辑。这些举措还带来了多项收购，成效显著。  （01:03:21）最后，令我印象深刻的是我们在应对各种变革时的敏捷性。每次面对新挑战时，我们都能灵活调整，令人惊叹。
举个例子，2020年我们决定加倍努力，致力于提供世界一流的云服务体验。为了实现这一目标，数百名员工在很短的时间内迅速行动起来，全力以赴地推进相关工作。这种高效执行的能力令人赞叹。我们从不犹豫砍掉那些没有前景的项目（此处有未听清的部分）。再举个例子：我们曾开发一款白板产品，本以为它会成为独立产品，类似于Jira的Product Discovery功能。但在与团队讨论该产品时，我们意识到它其实更像是一种实用的文档类型。如今，这项功能已整合至Confluence平台，整个决策过程异常迅速。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have this new segment, not that new anymore, called Failure Corner. I'm curious if you have any interesting story of a big failure in your career. And if you do, what you learned from that experience?
turns.zh: 我有个新栏目，虽然说也不算新了，叫做“失败角”。我想问问你们，是否有过职业生涯中重大的失败经历？如果有的话，又从中汲取了哪些教训？

turns.speaker: Megan Cook
turns.en: I think I'll give you a bit of a different one because I think this one is harder to spot and I think that's really interesting. It's something that I think about all the time though. So I missed a really big opportunity to move Atlassian forward back in the day. And I, like I said, think about it every time I review a new idea or look at an opportunity that we're thinking about. (01:05:06): So I was on this team and I was improving the way that our products help developers get their work done. And so typically we saw them start in Jira software. They'd pick up a piece of work and then they'd switch tools. They'd create a brand, they'd start writing code. And we noticed that they would forget to come back and update the status of their work and this could create a lot of confusion in the team. Another developer could pick up that work thinking it wasn't started and then there was a lot of wasted time. Or if you're trying to track metrics like how long does it take for a piece of work to get started through to done? That'll totally ski things. So this was causing a lot of problems. (01:05:42): But we didn't want to make developers come back into the tool that was obviously something that was getting in the way of their work. So we decided to build automation so they didn't have to leave their ID or the command line to do that. They can just keep working. So an example is Jira would detect that a new command had been created and then it could automatically move your piece of work to in progress because there's code being written against it. And there were a whole bunch of these examples that parties integrated into it and I made the decision to put into Jira as a user was editing their workflow and we shipped it and it performed just fine. People discovered it, they used it, and seemed to give a lot of value. People liked it, which doesn't really sound like a fail. I don't think that... (01:06:33): Where I dropped the ball was more about what I should have realized about that feature. So automation, it's super useful. It can be used by a whole slew of people who aren't just developers. It could be used in every single product. It's more than just moving things to a new status. And so I should have realized that we could have built this amazing service that every product could have moved themselves forward with. And years later, Atlassian actually acquired a company that did exactly that, this advanced automation. And it's in every product now. And so you can imagine how much it costs to acquire a company. That was a really extensive mistake on my part. So when I see a new idea, I'm always asking myself, "How do we push this further? Is there something there that we can 10X? Can we apply it more broadly to more types of users, more products? Is there some bigger opportunity that we can really take advantage of?"
turns.zh: 我觉得我要讲个稍微不同点的故事，因为这个失败案例更难被察觉，但我觉得挺有意思的。不过这事儿我也经常回想。早年间，我错失了一个推动Atlassian发展的重要机遇。就像我之前说的，每次评估新想法或审视我们正在考虑的机会时，我都会想起这件事。（01:05:06）：当时我在一个团队里，致力于提升我们的产品帮助开发者高效工作的能力。我们发现用户通常是从Jira软件开始的，他们接手一个任务后，会切换到其他工具。比如创建一个品牌，开始写代码。但我们注意到，他们往往会忘记回头更新任务状态，这会给团队带来很多混乱。其他开发者可能会误以为任务还没开始，浪费大量时间。或者如果你想追踪一个任务从开始到完成的耗时数据，那数据肯定会出错。这些问题实在太多了。（01:05:42）：但我们不想让开发者再回到那个明显阻碍他们工作的工具里。所以我们决定开发自动化功能，让他们无需离开当前界面就能操作。举个例子，Jira会检测到用户创建了新命令，然后自动将任务状态改为"进行中"，因为有代码在针对它进行开发。还有很多类似的例子，我们把它们集成到Jira中，当用户在编辑工作流时就能用上了。结果反响很好，大家都觉得很有价值。看起来这不像是失败啊，我觉得...（01:06:33）：我犯的错误在于，我本该更早意识到这个功能的潜力所在。自动化功能超级实用，不只是开发者能用，几乎所有产品都能用。这不只是把任务状态改来改去那么简单。我本该意识到，我们能打造出一个让所有产品都能自我提升的神奇服务。而多年后，Atlassian果然收购了一家做这种先进自动化技术的公司，现在每个产品都用上了这项功能。想想看收购一家公司的成本有多高，这真是我犯的重大失误。所以现在看到新想法时，我总会问自己："如何能把它推向更高层次？有没有什么可以放大10倍的潜力？能否让它适用于更多用户、更多产品？有没有更大的机遇值得我们把握？"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an awesome story. So the lesson there is just think bigger with the products. You almost need to wait for it to first be successful for you just to be like, "Oh, but can we do something more with this?" Do you think you should have been thinking about that as you were building it or would that have been too early?
turns.zh: 这故事太棒了。所以关键在于对产品要有更宏大的愿景。你得先等它成功，再去问自己："我们还能怎么做得更好？"你觉得开发时就该考虑这些吗？还是说那时考虑太早了？

turns.speaker: Megan Cook
turns.en: No, I think I should have caught that as we were building it, because even when I think about the experience, so it was a really good proving ground for it for sure. But even when I think about the experience, just where that experience was designed and product limited its functionality, which is a real shame.
turns.zh: 不是，我觉得我们在开发过程中本该发现这个问题的。即便现在回想起来，这次经历确实为我们提供了一个很好的验证平台。但当我回想整个过程时，设计体验和产品功能受限的地方实在令人遗憾。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I guess the takeaway there is just if you're committing to some idea, ask yourself what would it look like if this was 10 times bigger? If this was a bigger deal, can this apply to other things we're doing? Is that right?
turns.zh: 我想关键在于，如果你要致力于某个想法，不妨问问自己：如果这个项目规模扩大十倍会怎样？如果这是一个更重大的项目，它能否应用于我们正在进行的其他工作？对吧？

turns.speaker: Megan Cook
turns.en: Yeah. Where could this go in three years, five years? And should that change the way that you think about it now?
turns.zh: 是的。三年、五年后它能发展到什么程度？这是否应该改变你当前的思路？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great advice. Megan, is there anything else that you wanted to share or is there anything you wanted to leave listeners with before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 很棒的建议。梅根，在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想和听众分享的吗？或者有什么想留给他们的收获？

turns.speaker: Megan Cook
turns.en: I'll leave you with something. And it's just this practice that I've found really useful for my squad that we've implemented pretty recently, and especially with remote work and all of that. So like I said, we have limited time together, but what we put into place is something we called Fight Club. I'll probably get in trouble for talking about Fight Club. The first rule is you don't talk about fight club.
turns.zh: 我想分享一个我们团队最近实施的做法，我发现它非常有效，尤其是在远程工作的情况下。所以就像我之前说的，我们在一起的时间有限，但我们建立了一个叫做“搏击俱乐部”的机制。说这个可能会惹上麻烦。第一条规则是，绝不谈论搏击俱乐部。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Everyone knows that.
turns.zh: 大家都知道这条规则。

turns.speaker: Megan Cook
turns.en: It's 30 minutes every week. And it's just for myself, my engineering and my design leader, and we get together and we know that we're going in there to have a conflict. I think often when there's difficult conversations or those conflicts come up, you can put them off until they become much bigger. Or if somebody is conflict adverse, they can try to avoid having it at all. But by having a specific sort of time in your week for something like that, then you're sort of in that mindset. You know you're going in there to solve a hard problem. You know that there's going to be a disagreement and it makes it much better. And I think the relationship we all have is so much better because we get on top of these things early.
turns.zh: 每周30分钟。只有我、我的工程团队和设计负责人，我们聚在一起，知道我们要去解决一个难题。我发现当遇到困难的对话或冲突时，人们往往会拖延到问题变得更严重的时候，或者如果有人不喜欢冲突，他们可能会试图完全避免。但通过每周专门安排时间进行这样的讨论，你就能进入那种思维模式。你知道自己要去解决一个难题，知道会有分歧，这样效果会好很多。我认为我们团队的关系因此更加融洽，因为我们能尽早处理这些问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is super cool. It's like couples therapy or something where you're just like, "What issues do we have? Let's work through them right now." I love that. I love that. And it makes it okay to bring up things that are bothering you and things that you think need to change. And with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 这太棒了。就像情侣心理咨询一样，直接面对问题："我们有什么矛盾？现在就解决它们吧。" 我喜欢这样。我喜欢这样。这样一来，大家就能畅所欲言，提出困扰自己的问题和需要改进的地方。接下来是激动人心的闪电问答环节。你们准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Megan Cook
turns.en: Yes, can't wait. Let's do it.
turns.zh: 是的，迫不及待了。开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First question, what are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 第一个问题，请推荐两三本你向别人推荐最多的书？

turns.speaker: Megan Cook
turns.en: Look, I have a habit of sending books to everyone who reports to me every year just on a skill they're working on. So I've got a huge list that I actually send out, but the one that I send out the most to new PMs especially is just inspired by Marty Cagan. It holds up really well. It was recommended to me by my first boss, and it's just got a bunch of great tips in there, just great foundational knowledge. (01:10:49): More recently, what I've been sending out for my managers is Scaling People by Claire Hughes Johnson. I think that just came out within the last year actually, but it's just got an incredible amount of really useful tactical things, templates, all sorts of things that you can put into practice.
turns.zh: 听着，我每年都会给向我汇报的每个人送书，专门针对他们正在钻研的某项技能。所以我整理了一份庞大的书单，确实会发送出去，但我最常送给新晋项目经理的书，灵感来源于马蒂·卡根（Marty Cagan）的作品。这本书经受住了时间考验。它是我第一位上司推荐给我的，里面有很多实用建议和基础知识。（01:10:49）最近，我给管理者们推荐的书是克莱尔·休斯·约翰逊（Claire Hughes Johnson）的《扩展团队》。这本书实际上是去年才出版的，但里面有大量实用的战术方法、模板和可应用于实践的技巧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great choices. We have both in the bookshelf behind me. Both of them have been on the podcast. I wish I could see the whole list of books that you recommend to people. If you don't have this written out anywhere, you should publish some kind of blog or newsletter post of here's the skill and here's the book you recommend.
turns.zh: 选得真不错。我们书架后面有这两本书。它们都上过播客。我真希望能看到你推荐给人们的书单全貌。要是没写成书单，你应该写篇博客或者发篇通讯，讲讲需要哪项技能，再推荐对应书籍。

turns.speaker: Megan Cook
turns.en: Oh, that's a great idea. Yeah, I'm going to do that. Thanks.
turns.zh: 哦，这主意不错。好的，我会这么做。谢谢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right, you have a homework assignment. Okay, next question. What is the favorite recent movie or TV show you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 好的，你有作业要做了。下一个问题：你最近最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Megan Cook
turns.en: I am so late to TV, but Foundation is the one that I've been binging lately, and I think it's just this huge world. And I'm not usually one that gets super into sci-fi, but the way that it brings forward some of these ideas for what new technologies could mean... If you haven't seen it, and this is really spoiling it, one of the main characters or three of the main characters are actually clones of this emperor who rules the universe and decided to clone himself at three different stages of his life so that those people could continue rolling. And I think even that idea just invites the idea of what if we stretched out human life? What are the impact? How do things advance when you've got that same mindset and same people continue on? It's super compelling.
turns.zh: 我入坑电视剧太晚了，但最近一直在狂追《基地》系列。我通常不太爱看科幻片，但这部剧提出的新科技可能带来的影响……如果你没看过，我剧透一下：主角之一——三个主角——其实是统治宇宙的皇帝的克隆体，他在不同人生阶段克隆了自己，让这些克隆体继续执政。我觉得这个设定引发了人们对延长人类寿命的思考：会有什么影响？当人们拥有相同的思维模式和相同的克隆体时，社会会如何发展？这太吸引人了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Foundation, the show got ruined for me by reading the books many, many years ago, is one of my favorite sci-fi trilogy of all time. And then I was so excited for the show and has nothing to do with the books, basically. It's like the storyline is completely different, the core idea is the same as the only real. So I just got tired of it and stopped. But if you haven't read the books, I think you would love it. It's beautiful.
turns.zh: 是啊，我读过原著书多年前就被剧透了，但《基地》三部曲仍是我最喜欢的科幻系列之一。然后我对这部剧特别兴奋，但和书完全没关系。剧情完全不同，核心思想是一样的。所以我看烦了就停了。但如果你没读过书，我觉得你会喜欢的。书写得太棒了。

turns.speaker: Megan Cook
turns.en: Are the books better?
turns.zh: 书更好吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, the books are better. The books are always better, I think is a good rule of thumb.
turns.zh: 是啊，书更好。书永远更好，总的来说这是个不错的经验法则。

turns.speaker: Megan Cook
turns.en: Yeah, that is a good rule. I'll probably pick that up.
turns.zh: 是啊，这确实是个好法则。我可能会去看看。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I was like a teenager when I read them, so I don't know. Maybe they suck, but I think people love them. Highly recommend the books if you liked the show especially. Next question, do you have a favorite interview question that you'd like to ask candidates?
turns.zh: 是啊。我读这些书的时候还是个青少年，所以我也不知道。也许书很烂，但人们还是喜欢。如果你喜欢这部剧，强烈推荐书。下一个问题：你有没有最喜欢的面试问题想问候选人？

turns.speaker: Megan Cook
turns.en: I think it's an old one, but a great one on the subject of failure. I love to ask people about their biggest failure and I think it's a good way to get to know somebody because you can see how introspective they are, how much they think about what's happened and what they learned from it. It shows whether or not they can be vulnerable with you. You can see what they consider to be a big failure. Some people will list something that's not really a failure. And also you can see about whether they've got that growth mindset. So have they learned something from that? Have they applied it moving forward? (01:13:51): Weird rule that I've found is that a lot of the best hires that I've had has had big failure stories that they've worked through and learned from. And so I think that's great to see what they consider there, what the learnings are, but also in the solution you can also see how they tackle something like that. So are they the type of person who wants to go and forge something all by themselves? Are they the type of person who will pull together a community to figure something out? So you get that insight into their values and their approach from that question too, which is hugely useful.
turns.zh: 我觉得这是一个老生常谈的话题，但关于失败的讨论却很发人深省。我喜欢问别人他们最大的失败经历，我认为这是了解一个人的好方法，因为你能看到他们有多善于反思，如何回顾过往并从中吸取教训。这能显示出他们是否能在你面前展现脆弱的一面。你能了解他们眼中什么算重大失败。有些人列举的其实并非真正的失败经历。此外，你还能判断他们是否具备成长型思维模式。比如，他们是否从中有所收获并将其应用于未来？（01:13:51）：我发现一个奇特的规律——我招募过的最优秀的员工，往往都有克服重大挫折并从中成长的故事。因此，我认为通过这个问题，你不仅能了解他们眼中何为重大失败、能从中汲取哪些教训，还能观察他们解决问题的方式。比如，他们是想独自开创一番事业，还是会召集团队共同攻克难题？通过这些细节，你能深刻洞察他们的价值观和处事方式，这对招聘决策非常有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a favorite product you've recently discovered that you really love?
turns.zh: 你最近有没有发现特别喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Megan Cook
turns.en: Yeah. You might have to stop me from going on and on about this, but I recently got a smoker, a Traeger smoker for smoking meat. And just the unboxing experience was incredible. So you get this huge box, cardboard box, you open it up. If you reverse the cardboard box, it becomes like a play saloon that your kid can jump into and just mess around in which-
turns.zh: 有啊。我可能得克制自己别一直念叨这个，但我最近买了一个Traeger牌的烟熏炉用来熏肉。光是开箱体验就令人惊喜。你会收到一个巨大的纸箱，打开后它就像个儿童游戏屋，孩子可以跳进去玩耍——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that's cool.
turns.zh: 哇，太酷了。

turns.speaker: Megan Cook
turns.en: ... rather than just throwing it out, it becomes something really cool and useful. The set of instructions has a six-pack of beer at the top, just helps you understand how far through you should be through your six-pack as you're constructing it. You get some tools with it. And they're really good actually. They're not the usual kind of throwaway tools that you get in something to put together something like this. In addition to that sort of playful delightfulness in there, as you build it, you discover things along the way. So I opened up the hopper where you put in your wood pellets and there was a baseball cap, a tray of baseball cap in there, which was unexpected and really cool. And then the whole experience of actually using it once you've set it up is amazing. So it's all connected to my phone. I can just head to the beach and have some brisket going and come home and it's beautifully done. It just works. It's integrated. It's got integrated recipes. Yeah, I love that. I like that one.
turns.zh: ……而不是直接扔掉，它能变成既酷又实用的玩意儿。说明书顶部印着六罐啤酒，帮助你判断组装进度时喝到哪罐了。还附赠了不少工具，质量真的不错，不像普通的拼装玩具附赠的那些劣质工具。除了这种趣味性十足的体验，组装过程中还能有意外惊喜。比如，我打开放木屑的料斗时，里面藏着一顶棒球帽和一盘棒球帽，真是意外之喜。等组装完成后，实际使用体验也令人惊叹。它能与手机互联，我可以在海滩上烤些牛胸肉，回家后就能享用美味的成品。一切都无缝衔接，配方库也整合得很好。我太爱这款产品了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And salt. That sounds so delightful. Such a great product experience. I'm going to have to get one I think. I think we're going to sell some Traeger smokers.
turns.zh: 还有盐。听起来真是太棒了。这样的产品体验太棒了。我觉得我也得买一个。我觉得我们会卖出不少Traeger烟熏炉的。

turns.speaker: Megan Cook
turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Next question. Do you have a favorite life motto that you often come back to share with friends, either in work or in life?
turns.zh: 下一个问题。你有没有最喜欢的座右铭，经常在工作或生活中分享给朋友的？

turns.speaker: Megan Cook
turns.en: It's around maximizing joy. And what I mean by that is it's about finding what's important and leaning into it or finding what's annoying and turning it into something I enjoy. To give you a super small example is I'm terrible with keys. I will leave that thing all over the place. You'll find it in my cutlery drawer or whatever, and I'll never find it again. And I think an obvious solution to that could be to put a hook on the wall or something where you can just leave them and you go back to that and it's easy to find. But what gives me joy is not actually having to have keys at all. And so now I have a fingerprint reader on my front door and I feel a little bit like James Bond every time I enter my house and I can let people in if somebody needs to leave a package or something that's easy to do. So it was turning something annoying into something more joyful. (01:17:24): And I think the other thing there is just I really value keeping great relationships and increasing those relationships. And so I always make time for these amazing friends that I have that live in London, and we have this pact where every time either one of us goes to the others' continent, we'll go meet them there. So every time I go to Europe, which last year I was in Berlin, at one point in Amsterdam, and on the plane, they came over and we just hung out and had a great time. And so it's making sure that you make time for those important things.
turns.zh: 关键在于如何最大限度地获得快乐。我的理解是，要找到对自己重要的事物并全心投入，或是将那些令人烦恼的事物转化为乐趣。比如，我对钥匙的管理能力很差，总把它们随处乱放——你可能会在餐具抽屉里找到它们，再也找不回来。但显而易见的解决办法是，在墙上装个挂钩之类的，方便放置钥匙。可真正让我快乐的，是根本不需要钥匙。所以我现在家门上装了指纹识别器，每次进家门都感觉自己像詹姆斯·邦德一样酷。这样一来，如果有人需要放置包裹之类的，也能轻松处理。（01:17:24）另外，我非常重视维系良好的人际关系，并不断加深这些情谊。我总会抽出时间去看望住在伦敦的挚友们，我们约定，只要有人去对方大陆旅行，就一定要见面。所以去年我去欧洲时，先去了柏林，后来又到了阿姆斯特丹。飞机上他们过来和我相聚，玩得很开心。这就是确保自己有时间去经营那些重要关系。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along the same lines, final question related to creating more joy. I noticed a beautiful surfboard behind you. For somebody that's trying to surf and maybe not being successful, what's one tip you could share with listeners to improve their success with surfing?
turns.zh: 同样，最后一个关于创造更多快乐的问题。我注意到你身后有一块漂亮的冲浪板。对于那些想尝试冲浪却不太成功的人，你能给听众分享什么提升成功率的建议吗？

turns.speaker: Megan Cook
turns.en: Isn't surfing the most humbling sport that you've ever tried?
turns.zh: 冲浪难道不是你尝试过的最让人谦逊的运动吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I've tried a few times and yeah, I would say so.
turns.zh: 是的，我尝试过几次，确实如此。

turns.speaker: Megan Cook
turns.en: I think surfing's really interesting. I've never done a sport like it in that it's something that you have to really feel. So I find every time you learn and you think about surfing, you sort of feel it before you know how to do it. So even just being able to catch a wave, a green pace wave, you're paddling, you're paddling, you don't quite know where to be, you don't quite know how much to paddle for that wave, and you just have to sort of be successful a couple times before you get the feel for it. And it's the same with trying to find the right wave. When I looked at the ocean the first time to try and pick the wave and pick where to be, I couldn't even see the shape of it to find that right place. It took me just seeing a hundred waves to be able to do that. (01:19:15): So my best tip for surfing is get out there, keep doing it, do it over and over and over again. You will get better. You'll start to see all of these things that you've never noticed before. And get some friends. Get some friends out there, get surfing accountability buddy to make sure that you're getting out there often.
turns.zh: 我觉得冲浪非常有趣。它和其他运动不同，因为你必须用心去感受。每次学习冲浪时，你先是感受到那种感觉，然后才掌握技巧。比如，想要抓住绿波浪（适合初学者的浪型），你划水划水，却不知道该站到哪里位置，也不知道该划多少下才能抓住浪头。只有成功几次后，你才能掌握感觉。寻找合适浪点也是如此。我第一次看海浪想选浪点时，根本看不清浪形轮廓。直到我观察了上百个浪头，才掌握诀窍。（01:19:15）所以我对冲浪的最佳建议就是多去尝试，不断练习。这样你会进步，也会发现许多以前从未注意到的东西。再就是找些朋友一起。找些朋友一起去，让他们监督你，确保你经常去冲浪。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: He's the best buddy. Amazing. Megan, we've talked about play and safety and buy-in and fighting the good fight and adding new product lines, also surfing. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out and maybe follow up on some stuff? And how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 他是最棒的伙伴。太棒了。梅根，我们谈到了玩乐、安全、责任感、坚持正确的事业、开发新产品线，还有冲浪。最后两个问题。听众如果想联系你，获取更多信息，在哪里能找到你？听众又如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.speaker: Megan Cook
turns.en: The best place to find me is on LinkedIn. I'm Megan Cook on LinkedIn. You can also find me if you're a customer in the Atlassian community, if you want to have a chat. And I'm also on social media, so on X, you can find me there as well. And be useful to me. Look, any feedback, absolutely any feedback on Jira software, always hungry for that.
